title: Muscles of the gluteal region and posterior thigh (posterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the back of the sacrum and coccyx, and the sacrotuberous ligament.
Most fibers end in the iliotibial tract. The deep lower fibers reach the gluteal tuberosity of the femur.
Extends the thigh, most strongly from the flexed position, as in rising from a chair or climbing stairs. Laterally rotates the thigh.
hy: Injury to the inferior gluteal nerve, as in a posterior dislocation of the hip, makes it hard to rise from a chair and to climb stairs.

rows: Outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines.
Lateral surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.
Abducts and medially rotates the thigh. Keeps the pelvis level when the opposite foot is off the ground.
hy: If the superior gluteal nerve is injured, the pelvis drops on the opposite side when the person stands on the affected limb (Trendelenburg sign).
Gluteal injections are given into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock or, more safely, into gluteus medius at the ventrogluteal site, away from the sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels.

rows: Thickened lateral band of the fascia lata, from the iliac crest to the anterolateral (Gerdy) tubercle on the lateral condyle of the tibia.
Receives the insertions of tensor fasciae latae and most of gluteus maximus, and steadies the hip and the extended knee.
hy: Irritation where the tract crosses the lateral epicondyle of the femur, from friction or from compression of the tissue under it, causes pain on the outer side of the knee in runners and cyclists (iliotibial band syndrome).

structures.name: Long head of biceps femoris muscle
prompts: Long head of biceps femoris muscle

rows: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5 to S2).
Flexes the leg at the knee, extends the thigh at the hip, and laterally rotates the flexed leg.

structures.name: Short head of biceps femoris muscle
prompts: Short head of biceps femoris muscle

rows: Linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur.
Head of the fibula, with the long head.
Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (L5 to S2).
Flexes the leg at the knee and laterally rotates the flexed leg. It does not cross the hip.
Ischial tuberosity, with the long head of biceps femoris.
Upper part of the medial surface of the tibia, with sartorius and gracilis (pes anserinus).
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5 to S2).
Extends the thigh at the hip, flexes the leg at the knee, and medially rotates the flexed leg.
Posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia.
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5 to S2).
Extends the thigh at the hip, flexes the leg at the knee, and medially rotates the flexed leg.
hy: A Baker (popliteal) cyst is a swelling of the bursa between this tendon and the medial head of gastrocnemius. It often connects with the knee joint.

rows: Adductor part from the inferior ramus of the pubis and the ramus of the ischium. Hamstring part from the ischial tuberosity.
Adductor part on the linea aspera and the medial supracondylar line of the femur. Hamstring part on the adductor tubercle.
Adductor part by the obturator nerve (L2 to L4). Hamstring part by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L4).
Adducts the thigh. The adductor part also flexes the thigh and the hamstring part extends it.
hy: The gap between its two insertions is the adductor hiatus. The femoral artery and vein pass through it to the back of the knee, where they become the popliteal artery and vein.

rows: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis.
Upper part of the medial surface of the tibia, with sartorius and semitendinosus (pes anserinus).
Adducts the thigh, flexes the leg at the knee, and helps rotate the flexed leg medially.
Greater trochanter and the lateral lip of the linea aspera of the femur.
Patella through the quadriceps tendon, and through the patellar ligament the tibial tuberosity.
Extends the leg at the knee.
